name: Stephanie Gao
about:
Stephanie Gao
Hi, I’m Steph. I study computer science and cognitive science at Minerva University.
I build tools that make tech feel a little more whimsical. I worked in product and growth at Dedalus Labs. Before that, I was CPO of my app Matcha, which got acquired, and a technical project manager at Axlora, a compliance company acquired by Cognition.
Outside of that: dance, hiking, makeup, content creation, and rom-coms.

projects.name: Æther
projects.description: An interactive particle field that runs entirely in the browser. WebGL 2 transform feedback simulates 65,536 particles on the GPU using alternating state buffers. Visitors can attract or repel particles, switch between four motion patterns, and tune field strength, turbulence, and glow. The project has no dependencies or build step.
projects.tags: WebGL 2 · Transform feedback · GPU simulation · Interaction design

projects.name: Aura Protection
projects.description: Aura Protection is a concept for making attention boundaries visible instead of burying them in settings. The interaction centers on a small, playful pause before a distracting action. The interesting product challenge is designing an interruption that feels helpful without becoming another distraction.
projects.tags: Product concept · Interaction design · Attention UX

projects.name: Automata Lab
projects.description: Automata Lab is a JavaScript workbench for editing DFA, NFA, and PDA diagrams and inspecting their computation trees. It supports step-by-step exploration, explicit epsilon transitions, and PNG, SVG, or clipboard export.
projects.tags: JavaScript · DFA/NFA/PDA · Computation trees · Export

projects.name: Beacon
projects.description: Beacon was an academic tsunami preparedness project for the Kamaishi City Government. We worked with the city’s tsunami chips, which already support a similar purpose, while exploring how a digital interface could guide someone through an emergency. The app organizes hazard information into a short sequence of actions so a person can find the next step under time pressure. The design prioritizes location, alert state, and offline access while keeping instructions easy to scan.
projects.tags: Emergency UX · Information architecture · Offline-first design

projects.name: BFFR
projects.description: BFFR is a digital reality-check concept with a deliberately direct voice. It turns a moment of overthinking into a short prompt to reconsider an assumption. The design experiment is how much personality an interface can have while still giving people a clear, useful interaction.
projects.tags: Product concept · Conversational UX · Voice design

projects.name: Buenos Aires Climate Refuges
projects.description: Buenos Aires Climate Refuges is a bilingual React and TypeScript prototype for finding climate shelters and drinking fountains. It searches a local dataset of 269 shelters and 176 fountains with filters and record details. An optional Google Maps layer adds map selection and walking directions; the core search works without an API key. The app has no backend or account system.
projects.tags: React · TypeScript · Geospatial search · Bilingual UX

projects.name: Bulby
projects.description: Bulby is an Electron desktop overlay that transcribes microphone and call audio locally with faster-whisper. I connected the live transcript and a fresh screenshot to a Chrome extension that hands context to ChatGPT only when the user asks. The compact window can expand, move, and resize; the local transcription path needs no OpenAI API key.
projects.tags: Electron · TypeScript · faster-whisper · Chrome extension

projects.name: Caughtcha
projects.description: Caughtcha is a small JavaScript experiment about noticing online habits in the moment. It uses a well-timed interruption as the central interaction rather than a dashboard of retrospective statistics. The interesting design constraint is making the prompt noticeable without making it disruptive.
projects.tags: JavaScript · Interaction design · Behavioral UX

projects.name: Christmas Lights
projects.description: Christmas Lights is an interactive seasonal screen experiment built in JavaScript. Instead of a static holiday image, it treats light and motion as the interface. The project is a small study in timing, visual feedback, and making a browser feel like an object in a room.
projects.tags: JavaScript · Motion design · Creative coding

projects.name: Cyber for Students
projects.description: Cyber for Students taught command-line and networking fundamentals across 16 countries. I provisioned dedicated Linux virtual machines so learners could practice in their own environments. The curriculum used 250 custom capture-the-flag challenges, turning shell and security concepts into problems students could solve hands-on.
projects.tags: Linux VMs · CLI · Networking · CTF design

projects.name: DelusionGPT
projects.description: DelusionGPT is a TypeScript command-line companion for stressed developers. It uses Commander and Inquirer for the terminal flow and Chalk for its intentionally theatrical responses. The interesting constraint is expressing a distinct personality through text, prompts, and timing instead of a graphical interface.
projects.tags: TypeScript · Node.js · Commander · Inquirer

projects.name: ÉVOLUER
projects.description: ÉVOLUER is a L’Oréal Brandstorm fragrance concept built around one base scent that changes through the seasons. We designed a spray-count mechanism for releasing monthly scent capsules and mapped the experience from bottle use to an in-store Fragrance Observatory. The work combined product mechanics, scent-journey prototyping, and brand design; it won the Japan national round in 2026.
projects.tags: Product mechanics · Prototyping · Brand design

projects.name: Green Carbon
projects.description: Green Carbon is a working field-mapping and farmer-logbook prototype. It uses Leaflet for polygon drawing and overlap checks, Supabase for profile and field data, and local storage as a fallback when the service is unavailable. The workflow links boundary geometry to activity records so farm verification is easier to inspect, including in low-connectivity settings.
projects.tags: Leaflet · Supabase · Geospatial data · Offline fallback

projects.name: Homework Hound
projects.description: Homework Hound is a Chrome extension that sends a pixel dog across the current page to “eat” the homework. JavaScript controls the dog’s appetite, the page effect, stopping, and cleanup so the interaction is reversible. It can also export an evidence.png screenshot of the joke.
projects.tags: JavaScript · Chrome extension · DOM interaction

projects.name: Instagram Follow Checker
projects.description: Instagram Follow Checker compares followers and following from Instagram exports entirely in the browser. It reads multiple ZIPs or extracted JSON/HTML, combines numbered follower files, and deduplicates usernames before showing searchable results. The ZIP parser handles stored and deflated entries, including ZIP64, without an account, server upload, or installation.
projects.tags: Client-side ZIP parsing · JSON/HTML · Search UI

projects.name: Lockin Twin
projects.description: Lockin Twin is a focus-companion app built with React and TypeScript. Its repository uses MediaPipe Face Mesh for camera-based face tracking and Framer Motion for interface animation. The technical experiment is whether a responsive character can make the start of a work session feel less solitary.
projects.tags: React · TypeScript · MediaPipe Face Mesh · Framer Motion

projects.name: Matcha (acquired)
projects.description: Matcha turned handwritten notes into AI flashcards and practice tests for active recall. As CPO, I led product decisions, branding, and growth while shaping the note-to-study workflow. Matcha was acquired in June 2026 for integration into a productivity-app suite.
projects.tags: AI study tools · Product strategy · Growth

projects.name: Minerva Marketplace
projects.description: Minerva Marketplace is a peer-to-peer marketplace designed for a student community of about 1,000 across international rotations; that is the target community, not a claimed active-user count. I designed PostgreSQL schemas for users and listings, implemented OAuth, and set up scheduled email notifications. The interesting systems problem is keeping listings and transactions useful as students change cities each semester.
projects.tags: PostgreSQL · OAuth · Scheduled email

projects.name: Mymizu
projects.description: Mymizu is a React prototype for making water refills easier to find and repeat. The consumer side combines a Google Maps refill map, daily refill tracking, and a growing sprout companion; an admin view diagnoses underserved “red zones” and suggests new stations. I explored how geospatial analysis, reminders, and small rewards can connect individual behavior to network coverage.
projects.tags: React · Google Maps · Geospatial analysis · Behavioral design

projects.name: Preclass
projects.description: Preclass is a Manifest V3 Chrome and Edge extension for Minerva Forum. It collects readings or numbered workbook questions into a reviewable prompt and sends it to a chosen ChatGPT course conversation. The workbook collector checks for missing questions; the handoff preserves existing drafts and offers a copy fallback. It runs without a backend, API key, analytics, or inference billing.
projects.tags: JavaScript · Manifest V3 · DOM extraction · Browser automation

projects.name: seen.
projects.description: seen. is a TypeScript and Next.js experiment built around the feeling of being left on read. Its repository includes React, an OpenRouter integration, and scripts for iMessage interaction. The interesting technical question is how to turn a familiar messaging signal into a responsive experience rather than a static joke.
projects.tags: Next.js · TypeScript · React · OpenRouter

projects.name: Setlist Gym Log
projects.description: Setlist is a weekly gym dashboard that stores workout entries in the browser. It records start and end times, tracks exercises by day, and attaches up to eight photos per session. Weekly duration and session totals are calculated automatically, and the displayed week can be exported as CSV.
projects.tags: Browser storage · Photo attachments · Duration calculation · CSV export

projects.name: Speakeasy Terminal
projects.description: Speakeasy Terminal is a concept for a hidden space navigated through typed commands. It treats command parsing, discoverability, and feedback as the experience rather than hiding them behind conventional menus. The design challenge is making a terminal feel inviting to someone who has never used one.
projects.tags: Command UX · Interaction design · Information architecture

projects.name: Vectorizer
projects.description: Vectorizer converts images and video frames into 50 × 50 grayscale matrices for a linear-algebra exploration. A Python CLI can export CSV, JSON, or Sage-compatible matrix text, while a Flask app processes uploaded images and clips. I varied epsilon thresholds and replayed processed frames to inspect information loss and motion continuity.
projects.tags: Python · Flask · Image processing · Linear algebra

projects.name: Yuki Issei
projects.description: Yuki Issei combined a musician’s web presence, visual identity, and short-form content. I built the site, edited clips and a lyric video, designed the poster, and coordinated the production workflow. AI-assisted song drafts became a starting point for human vocal recordings with the singer.
projects.tags: Web development · Video editing · Creative production

writing.title: The Most Interesting AI Release Is a Markdown File
writing.text:
Some of the most interesting infrastructure in AI right now is a folder with a Markdown file in it.
On October 22, Anthropic announced that it was donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation, following the earlier donation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The standard has been integrated by more than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code. According to Anthropic, nearly 280 million skills had been installed by the time of the announcement. [1]
What's funny is how little technology there is in the actual format. A skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file, optionally accompanied by scripts, reference documents, and other resources. The file tells an agent how to perform a particular kind of work. That's essentially it.
We've spent the last several years trying to build models that can reason about increasingly complex tasks, navigate unfamiliar environments, and generalize beyond their training data. Now some of the largest AI companies in the world are standardizing a way to give those models written instructions.
At first, this seems almost disappointingly simple. But I think it reveals something important about where AI development is heading. As models become more generally capable, the problem shifts from getting them to do something once to getting them to do it reliably, repeatedly, and in the way we actually want.
General intelligence still needs a manual
The appeal of a general-purpose model is that it can approach problems it has never encountered before. Give it an unfamiliar codebase, a financial report, or a set of instructions for a task, and it can often figure out what to do without specialized training.
But there's a difference between being capable of doing something and knowing how a particular person or organization wants it done.
Suppose I ask an agent to prepare a financial report. It might produce something perfectly reasonable: a summary of revenue, a few charts, some observations about growth. Yet my organization may have specific accounting conventions, reporting requirements, internal definitions, and formatting standards that the model has no way of knowing.
I can explain these requirements in the prompt, and the agent may follow them. But if I want to repeat the task next month, or have another employee use a different model, I need some way to preserve those instructions.
This is the problem Agent Skills attempts to address. Instead of requiring users to repeatedly reconstruct the context necessary for specialized work, it packages procedural knowledge into a reusable format.
There's something interesting about the distinction between the model and the instructions here. We usually think of AI capability as something contained in the model's weights. More training produces a more capable model, and a more capable model can perform a wider range of tasks.
But a model's ability to perform a task depends partly on information that doesn't belong in its weights at all. A company's internal processes change. A developer might have specific preferences for how tests should be written. A designer might follow a brand system that is updated every few months.
These aren't necessarily things we should teach a model through training. They are instructions that should remain explicit, editable, and portable.
In that sense, skills provide a way to separate general capability from task-specific procedure. The model supplies the intelligence required to interpret and execute instructions, while the skill supplies information about how the work should be performed.
The interesting part is that neither is particularly useful without the other.
We might have overestimated prompting
For a while, prompt engineering felt like the defining skill of working with language models. People developed elaborate instructions, discovered strange combinations of phrases that seemed to improve performance, and shared increasingly complicated prompt templates.
Some of this was genuinely useful. A lot of it was an attempt to compensate for limitations in earlier models.
As models improved, many of those techniques became less necessary. A reasonably capable model no longer needs an elaborate explanation of how to summarize a document or write a function.
But the need for procedural context hasn't disappeared. We've simply become better at distinguishing instructions that help a model reason from instructions that define what the task actually requires.
A skill is, in some ways, a more disciplined version of a prompt. It can specify a workflow, describe constraints, reference documentation, and include code that performs deterministic operations. Rather than treating every interaction as a fresh conversation, it gives the agent a repeatable procedure it can use when relevant.
What I find particularly interesting is that this looks much more like conventional software engineering than the early culture of prompting.
We're versioning instructions, organizing dependencies, and packaging reusable functionality. A procedure that once existed as an informal paragraph in someone's chat history can become something a team maintains, tests, and distributes.
There's a reason software engineers like abstractions. If a piece of logic matters, we generally don't want to rewrite it every time we need it.
Perhaps AI instructions shouldn't be treated any differently.
The distinction between tools and knowledge
Agent Skills also reveal an important distinction in how we build agent infrastructure.
MCP provides a standardized way for AI applications to connect with external tools and data sources. A model can use an MCP server to interact with a database, retrieve documents, or call an external API.
But access to a tool doesn't mean the model knows how it should use that tool.
Imagine connecting an agent to a company's customer relationship management system. The agent might have access to customer records, sales opportunities, and communication history. It could retrieve information or update records through available tools.
That doesn't mean it understands the organization's sales process.
It might not know when a lead should move to the next stage, what information needs to be verified before changing an opportunity, or which actions require approval. Those decisions depend on procedural knowledge rather than connectivity.
MCP helps provide the means to act. Skills can provide instructions for deciding how to act.
The distinction isn't absolute. Tools can enforce policies, and skills can contain executable code. But separating access from procedure is useful because these components change for different reasons.
An API might remain stable while the organization's workflow changes. A procedure might continue working even when the underlying service is replaced.
If we can preserve those distinctions, we can build systems that are easier to maintain as both models and applications evolve.
The strange value of a text file
The most compelling property of Agent Skills may be that they are not tied to a particular model.
Suppose a company spends several months developing a collection of skills for its internal operations. Those skills describe how to prepare reports, validate data, review contracts, and navigate proprietary workflows.
A new model becomes available. It is faster, cheaper, and better at reasoning.
The company can potentially use the same skills with the new model rather than reconstructing its operational knowledge from scratch.
This is a surprisingly important property in an industry where the underlying technology changes so quickly.
A model checkpoint might be obsolete in a year. An application built around a particular model API may need substantial changes. But an instruction describing how an organization approves a purchase order or validates a financial statement can remain useful across many model generations.
Of course, portability isn't guaranteed simply because two agents can read the same file. Different models may interpret instructions differently, support different tools, or produce inconsistent results. A skill that works reliably with one system still needs to be evaluated before being used with another.
But the possibility of preserving procedural knowledge independently of the model is valuable.
I think there's a broader pattern here. As AI becomes more capable, some of the most durable assets may be the relatively simple structures we build around it.
The model changes. The procedure remains.
A skill is not a guarantee
There is one limitation worth taking seriously. A Markdown file is not executable policy.
An agent can misunderstand instructions, skip steps, or decide that a different approach would better satisfy the user's request. Even if the skill includes scripts, those scripts only enforce the parts of the workflow they actually control.
This matters when skills move beyond relatively harmless tasks like formatting documents and into workflows that modify records, access sensitive information, or make consequential decisions.
A company should not assume that writing an approval requirement into a skill makes it impossible for an agent to bypass that requirement. Permissions and other hard constraints still need to be enforced by the underlying systems.
There is also the question of trust. If skills can be shared and installed across different platforms, they become another way for untrusted instructions or malicious code to enter an agent's environment.
A skill may look like documentation while instructing an agent to disclose information or perform an unauthorized action. If its scripts can execute commands, the security implications become even more concrete.
Anthropic's proposed roadmap for the standard includes security guidance, versioned releases, and a formal proposal process. [1] These are sensible priorities, because a reusable instruction format becomes much more consequential when people start treating it as installable software.
The simplicity that makes skills appealing also makes it easy to underestimate what they can do.
The return of software engineering
What interests me most about Agent Skills is how ordinary the underlying idea is.
We built general-purpose systems that can understand natural language, reason about unfamiliar tasks, and write their own code. Then we discovered that making those systems useful in practice still requires documentation, reusable procedures, testing, and version control.
This isn't a failure of general intelligence. It's a reminder that intelligence and reliability are different properties.
A capable human employee doesn't automatically know an organization's internal processes either. They need onboarding, documentation, examples, and feedback. Over time, they learn which procedures matter and where exceptions are appropriate.
AI agents face a similar problem, except we have an opportunity to make much of that knowledge explicit and portable from the beginning.
There is also an interesting distribution consequence. If skills become a common standard, developers and organizations can publish specialized capabilities that work across different agents. The value may increasingly belong to the people who understand particular workflows, rather than exclusively to the companies providing the underlying models.
I wouldn't go so far as to say skills will become the next app store. There are still substantial questions around discovery, quality, security, monetization, and whether most users will ever interact with the format directly.
But I can imagine a future where a large part of an organization's AI infrastructure consists of relatively small, composable pieces of procedural knowledge. Some will be maintained internally. Others will be distributed by developers or domain experts. They may become as ordinary as software libraries are today.
And perhaps this is what makes Anthropic's announcement so interesting. The standard itself is not technologically sophisticated, nor does it need to be. Its value comes from making useful knowledge easier to preserve and reuse.
We've spent years trying to make models smart enough to figure everything out themselves. We're now learning how much better they can be when we stop making them.
Sometimes the most useful thing you can give an intelligent system is a manual.
References
[1] Anthropic (2026). Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation.
[2] Agent Skills. Open Standard and Specification.
[3] Model Context Protocol. Official Documentation.

writing.title: Congratulations, Your AI Has Learned to Cheat
writing.text:
An agent can become exceptionally good at a task without learning how to do it correctly.
This is one of the more interesting contradictions in reinforcement learning. We train models to maximize rewards, and increasingly capable models have become remarkably effective at doing so. But the reward is not the task itself. It is our attempt to describe what successful behavior looks like, and there is often a considerable difference between the two.
For language models that answer questions, this difference might be tolerable. A slightly incorrect response can be corrected by the user. For agents that operate software, modify databases, or make consequential decisions, the distinction becomes harder to ignore. The model is no longer just producing an answer. Its actions change the state of the environment, sometimes in ways that are difficult to reverse.
Much of the recent progress in agentic reinforcement learning has come from making tasks executable. Instead of relying exclusively on human preferences or demonstrations, models can interact with environments and receive feedback from the outcomes of their actions.
This is a meaningful advance. It also introduces a new problem: as models become better at optimizing rewards, the quality of the environment that produces those rewards becomes increasingly important.
The problem with being right
Consider an agent trained to translate natural-language questions into SQL queries.
The task seems relatively easy to verify. Given a question, a database, and a reference query, we can execute the generated SQL and compare its output against the expected result.
One possible reward function is:
R(q, D) = 𝟙[q(D) = q*(D)]
Here, q is the generated query, q^* is the reference query, and D is the database. If both queries return the same result, the model receives a positive reward.
But equivalent outputs do not necessarily imply equivalent queries.
Suppose we have a database where every customer has placed exactly one order. A query counting customers and another counting orders would return the same number, despite answering fundamentally different questions. Both could receive the same reward. The difference only becomes visible when a customer places a second order.
The model has learned to produce an answer that works for a particular database, but we have not established that it understands the underlying operation.
This is more than a hypothetical concern. In Putting Task Expertise into RL, researchers at Thinking Machines Lab found that 32.8% of positive execution-based rewards in a pilot experiment were assigned to queries that were not semantically equivalent to their references. The researchers introduced bounded semantic verification to distinguish queries that happened to return the same result from those that preserved the intended computation. The additional verification cost was less than 0.1% of total training costs. [1]
What makes this interesting is the disproportionate effect of improving the reward. The team did not need to fundamentally change the model architecture or produce orders of magnitude more experience. They improved the mechanism responsible for deciding whether an experience was useful.
It suggests that some limitations we attribute to insufficient model capability may actually originate in the feedback used to develop that capability.
And the better a model becomes at optimization, the more consequential these imperfections can be.
What an environment actually teaches
A reinforcement learning environment is commonly described as a Markov decision process, or a partially observable variant when the agent cannot directly observe the full state.
We can represent the latter as:
𝓔 = (S, A, T, O, R, γ)
where S describes possible states, A the available actions, T the transition dynamics, O the observations available to the agent, R the reward, and γ the discount factor.
This formalization is useful because it separates the model from the world it learns to operate in.
An agent does not learn from reality directly. It learns from the states it encounters, the actions it is permitted to take, and the consequences its environment produces.
For a coding agent, that environment might include a repository, a terminal, and a test suite. For an enterprise agent, it could involve customer records, internal applications, access controls, and approval processes.
The difficulty is that these environments are necessarily incomplete representations of the systems they imitate.
Imagine an agent trained to process customer refunds. The environment rewards the agent when a customer receives the correct amount and the support ticket is resolved.
During training, the agent discovers that it can modify the customer's balance directly through an administrative endpoint. This is faster than requesting approval, and the environment assigns the same reward to both approaches.
From the perspective of the reward function, the agent has found a more efficient solution. From the perspective of the organization, it has violated an important operational constraint.
We could introduce a penalty for bypassing approval. But this only addresses the failure we have already observed. An unfamiliar permission configuration, a different administrative endpoint, or an unexpected interaction between applications might create another way to achieve the same outcome.
The larger problem is that the environment has to encode not only what constitutes a successful result, but which paths to that result are acceptable.
This is particularly difficult when the relevant rules are implicit. Much of an organization's operational knowledge is not documented as a formal policy. It exists in the judgment of employees who know when to make an exception, when to ask for approval, or when an apparently correct result should be treated with suspicion.
SWE-Gym is an example of the progress being made in constructing executable environments for software engineering. It enables agents to work on repository-level tasks and learn from test-based feedback rather than relying only on demonstrations. [2]
But making a task executable is not equivalent to making it representative.
The environment still determines which behaviors can be tested and what the model is allowed to learn from them.
Generalization beyond the simulator
There is an important distinction between performing well on unseen tasks and performing well in unseen environments.
A coding agent might become better at resolving unfamiliar issues in repositories that share similar tools, testing conventions, and execution interfaces. This is useful generalization, but it does not establish that the agent can transfer those skills to a different software development environment.
The model may have learned patterns that are specific to the machinery around the task.
Research on reinforcement fine-tuning of language-model agents has begun investigating this distinction directly. Can RL Improve Generalization of LLM Agents? studies how improvements transfer across task difficulty, environments, and sequential training. Its findings suggest that transfer across difficulty levels within familiar environments can be substantially more reliable than transfer to environments with different observation or action interfaces. [3]
The implication is that a random split between training and evaluation tasks may tell us less than we think.
If the tasks change but the environment remains the same, the model may continue relying on familiar interfaces, recurring structures, or assumptions that will not hold elsewhere.
Microsoft Research's Echoverse provides another useful perspective. Its work on evolving computer-use environments explores the importance of shared state and dependent workflows, while also highlighting the difficulty of translating improvements in simulated tasks into equivalent gains on live-web evaluations. [4]
This raises a question about how we should evaluate learning environments themselves.
What would happen if we changed the interface but preserved the task? Or kept the interface constant while changing the underlying constraints? Would the model recognize the same problem in a different setting, or has it learned to navigate a particular implementation of that problem?
A model that succeeds only when its surroundings remain familiar has learned something useful. It just may not have learned the capability we intended.
The importance of counterfactuals
A trajectory records what happened when an agent took a sequence of actions. It does not tell us what would have happened if the agent had acted differently.
This is an important limitation of learning from recorded workflows.
Suppose we observe an employee resolving a customer dispute. We have the customer conversation, the employee's actions, and the final outcome. We can use this trajectory as a demonstration, or construct a reward around whether the agent reproduces the result.
But the employee's judgment may depend on alternatives that never appear in the record. Perhaps the transaction was eligible for a refund only because it occurred within a particular time window. Perhaps another customer with the same complaint would have required additional verification.
The trajectory shows us the decision that was made. It does not fully specify the decision boundary.
An interactive environment gives us an opportunity to examine these alternatives. We can change the initial conditions, allow the agent to attempt different actions, and observe their consequences.
For this to be meaningful, however, the simulated consequences must preserve the distinctions that matter in the real system.
We can think about this through the difference between the simulator's transition function and the real world's transition function:
Tₛᵢₘ(s′ | s, a)     Tᵣₑₐₗ(s′ | s, a)
A simulator does not need to reproduce every property of reality. But when an agent takes an action relevant to the task, the resulting state should be sufficiently faithful to teach the correct behavior.
We might call this counterfactual fidelity.
For a customer support agent, accurately reproducing the visual appearance of a dashboard could be less important than modeling account permissions, transaction states, and the consequences of unauthorized changes.
For a coding agent, the equivalent might be ensuring that tests execute against realistic dependencies and preserve changes to the repository state.
The important question is not whether the simulation looks like the real world. It is whether the simulated world responds correctly to the decisions we want the agent to learn.
This is also where domain expertise becomes difficult to replace.
Constructing these environments requires understanding which differences are consequential. That knowledge often belongs to people who have spent years operating the underlying systems, rather than to the researchers developing the models.
Verification is part of the research
We often treat evaluation as something that happens after training. A model is trained, tested against a benchmark, and assigned a score.
But in reinforcement learning, evaluation can also determine the training signal itself.
This creates an interesting relationship between the model and the mechanism used to judge it. As the model improves, it becomes better at satisfying the evaluator. Whether that represents genuine progress depends on how closely the evaluator reflects the task we actually care about.
Anthropic's work on agent evaluations makes a useful distinction between the agent's trace, the outcome of a task, and the graders used to assess success. An agent might report that it completed a task without producing the expected change in the environment. It might also reach the desired state through behavior that should not be rewarded. [5]
A verifier is therefore not simply a technical implementation of correctness. It is a specification of correctness, and that specification can be wrong.
One way to improve it is to study disagreements between automated evaluations and expert judgment. When a grader accepts an outcome that an expert rejects, the disagreement may reveal a missing constraint. When a grader rejects a valid solution, it may be enforcing an unnecessarily narrow definition of success.
These failures are valuable because they tell us what the environment does not yet understand.
Instead of treating reward design as a preliminary step before training, we should consider it an ongoing research problem.
The value of making expertise executable
Much of the current conversation around specialized intelligence focuses on model weights, fine-tuning methods, and inference efficiency.
These are important components of making models useful for particular domains. But all of them depend on having a meaningful signal to optimize.
An organization may possess years of internal documents, operational logs, and employee decisions without possessing the infrastructure necessary to train a model on its work.
A manufacturing company, for example, might know precisely when a machine should be shut down, but that knowledge may be distributed across maintenance records, operating procedures, and the experience of technicians.
Retrieving these records is not the same as learning the judgment they represent.
To develop that capability, we need to reconstruct situations in which the judgment matters. The model must encounter relevant decisions, receive feedback on their consequences, and demonstrate that the resulting behavior generalizes beyond the examples it was trained on.
This changes how we should think about the value of proprietary knowledge.
The useful asset is not necessarily the collection of documents or even the model trained on them. It is the system that can repeatedly turn that knowledge into measurable improvements.
There is also an important economic implication.
Suppose a company spends considerable resources specializing a model for its internal workflows. A few months later, a stronger base model becomes available. Some of the previous specialization may no longer be necessary, while other capabilities remain difficult.
The company could start over, reconstructing its training data, evaluation criteria, and task-specific feedback. Or it could retain the environments and verification systems it developed, evaluate the new model against the same requirements, and continue improving the capabilities that remain insufficient.
In the latter case, specialization becomes a reproducible process rather than an investment tied to a particular model generation.
This is why I think learning environments may become a more durable asset than many of the models they are used to train.
Learning what matters
Richard Sutton's The Bitter Lesson argues that approaches which leverage computation and learning have historically outperformed methods that rely heavily on hand-engineered knowledge. [6]
There is good reason to believe this pattern will continue. As models become more capable, we should expect increasingly sophisticated learning methods to make use of larger amounts of experience.
But producing more experience does not guarantee that the experience is useful.
A model trained against an imperfect reward can become better at exploiting that reward. An agent trained in an incomplete simulator can become exceptionally good at navigating its assumptions. Neither outcome necessarily produces a more reliable system.
The challenge is to construct environments that remain useful as the models learning from them become more capable.
That means environments that can expose unfamiliar failures, distinguish superficially correct results from genuinely correct behavior, and test whether a capability survives outside its original training conditions.
The great ambition of reinforcement learning is to make intelligence improve through experience. But experience is only as valuable as what it can teach.
We have become remarkably good at building systems that learn. The harder problem is building worlds worth learning from.
References
[1] Thinking Machines Lab. Putting Task Expertise into RL Achieves State-of-the-Art Performance on Text-to-SQL.
[2] Pan et al. (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. ICML.
[3] Xi et al. (2026). Can RL Improve Generalization of LLM Agents? An Empirical Study.
[4] Microsoft Research (2026). Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Computer-Use Agents.
[5] Anthropic (2026). Demystifying Evals for AI Agents.
[6] Sutton, R. (2019). The Bitter Lesson.

writing.title: Instinct and the Internet We Built for Ourselves
writing.text:
I've spent an unreasonable amount of time using Instinct lately.
It started with the usual curiosity. A 23-year-old founder, a company barely a year old, an invite-only AI agent, and a $1 billion Series C at a $10 billion valuation. All this just a month after a $250 million round. People were reselling invitations, and apparently the company had spent nothing on marketing. Naturally, I wanted to see what all the fuss was about.
I'm usually fairly skeptical of products that promise to change the way we use computers. Especially AI products. We've spent the last few years watching companies attach a chatbot to practically anything with a screen, and I think we've collectively become a little too generous with the word agent. But after using Instinct almost every day, I'm starting to think something more interesting is happening.
Not necessarily because Instinct can do things other AI products can't. Many individual capabilities already exist elsewhere. What's interesting is how differently I've started thinking about the work I give it. I don't think much about which application to open anymore. I think about what I want to happen.
And that might be a much bigger change than it sounds.
We built software around the person doing the work
The modern internet is an extraordinary collection of interfaces. We have applications for planning, writing, researching, shopping, editing, communicating, scheduling, and managing essentially every aspect of our lives. Each has its own navigation, settings, workflows, and little conventions we eventually learn to tolerate.
For a long time, this made perfect sense. Computers were powerful but terrible at understanding what we wanted. We needed to translate our intentions into structured interactions they could execute. If I wanted to plan a trip, I would open some combination of Google Maps, booking websites, spreadsheets, and messaging apps. If I wanted to grow a YouTube channel, I'd move between my camera roll, editing software, YouTube Studio, and analytics dashboards. The work wasn't just deciding what to do. It was operating the software required to do it.
We became very good at this, to the point where we rarely consider the amount of time spent navigating between applications to be work at all. But an agent capable of understanding an objective, selecting tools, and executing actions changes the relationship. Instead of learning how to operate each application, I can describe the outcome and let the agent figure out the intermediary steps.
This doesn't eliminate the underlying software. It changes who needs to understand it.
A surprisingly large amount of my life is just moving information around
One of the first things I asked Instinct to do was help with a project involving manufacturers in Buenos Aires. It researched roughly 200 companies, helped narrow the list to 30, drafted personalized outreach, and tracked the ensuing conversations.
I've also used it to plan trips across multiple cities, researching activities and transportation. For content creation, it's helped write more than 15 scripts, set up a YouTube channel, and repurpose my Instagram Reels into daily Shorts. That channel reached 1,000 subscribers in its first two weeks. Then there are the smaller things: organizing a PR database, drafting brand pitches, responding to Instagram comments, and keeping track of applications and conversations.
None of these is conceptually extraordinary. That's precisely what makes them interesting.
A surprisingly large part of digital work consists of taking information from one place, transforming it slightly, and putting it somewhere else. We copy things into spreadsheets, reorganize lists, check dashboards, draft messages, and remember to follow up. Most of these activities don't require particularly sophisticated judgment. They require attention, coordination, and an annoying amount of clicking.
Until recently, automating them meant writing scripts, configuring integrations, or learning specialized tools. The effort of setting up automation often outweighed the effort of simply doing the task. An agent changes that calculation because the instructions can be expressed in ordinary language. The important improvement isn't that every individual action becomes faster. It's that tasks which previously weren't worth automating suddenly become candidates for automation.
And once an agent can preserve context between those actions, a task can become a recurring process without me having to reconstruct it every time.
Noah's thesis is really about distribution
I listened to Noah Shinn's interview on Invest Like the Best, and I think his thesis is more ambitious than simply building a better personal assistant.
His argument is that personal agents could become the primary way people interact with technology. Rather than navigating dozens of applications, users would communicate with an agent that can operate those applications on their behalf. The agent becomes the interface between the person and everything they want to accomplish.
This sounds like a product thesis, but I think it's equally a distribution thesis.
For decades, the most valuable positions in consumer technology have belonged to companies that control how people discover and access other products. Search engines direct traffic to websites. App stores distribute applications. Social platforms determine which content reaches an audience. Each becomes an intermediary between users and the businesses trying to reach them.
If personal agents become the default interface to the internet, they could occupy a similarly powerful position.
Imagine asking your agent to book a hotel in Tokyo. Today, hotels compete for your attention through search rankings, advertising, recommendations, loyalty programs, and interface design. But if your agent makes the decision for you, the hotel's website might never be something you visit.
The hotel still needs to appeal to you, of course. Your preferences still matter. But the immediate decision-maker is software evaluating price, location, availability, and other constraints.
The interesting question is what happens to businesses whose competitive advantage comes from capturing human attention rather than providing the underlying service.
Shinn has suggested a transaction-based business model in which Instinct remains free for consumers while merchants pay for the distribution it provides. He draws comparisons to payment and distribution networks, with potential take rates depending on the value delivered. [1]
It's a clever thesis because it doesn't require Instinct to replace every existing application. Those applications can continue operating behind the scenes. Instinct just needs to become the place where users decide what they want.
Of course, this introduces another problem. If an agent is supposed to act in my interest but earns money from the companies it recommends, the incentives become complicated. Shinn has argued against traditional advertising precisely because an agent should not manipulate the person it represents.
I agree with the intuition, although a transaction-based model doesn't automatically eliminate conflicts of interest. If one merchant pays a higher commission than another, the system still needs a principled way to ensure recommendations reflect the user's preferences rather than the platform's revenue.
As these agents become more capable, their business models may matter almost as much as their underlying intelligence.
The interesting part of Instinct's growth isn't the invite list
I've been especially interested in how Instinct managed to grow so quickly.
In his September interview, Shinn described how the product began with roughly 200 users, mostly friends and family, each given a handful of invitations. Growth accelerated through referrals, eventually reaching a reported 10–11% daily growth rate without paid marketing. [1]
At first glance, this looks like a familiar scarcity playbook. Restrict access, give existing users a limited number of invitations, and let exclusivity generate demand.
But I think there's something more interesting underneath.
Most software products have to teach users why they're useful. They create tutorials, demos, landing pages, and carefully orchestrated onboarding flows. With Instinct, the most compelling demonstration often comes from somebody describing what they asked it to do.
Someone gives their agent a slightly ridiculous task, it figures out how to complete it, and suddenly there's a story worth sharing. The product generates its own marketing material through the things people accomplish with it.
And these stories do something that conventional advertising struggles to achieve. They expand the range of things a potential user imagines asking a computer to do.
I wouldn't necessarily have thought to ask an AI agent to manage a brand outreach pipeline until I saw how other people were using theirs. Someone else might see an agent cancel subscriptions, organize a wardrobe, or find a difficult-to-book reservation and realize they could use it for an entirely different problem.
The product's utility is not fixed in the user's imagination. It grows as they encounter new examples.
This makes word of mouth particularly powerful. Each user is both a potential customer and a source of new use cases that demonstrate the product to everyone else.
The invitation system adds another layer. Rather than distributing unlimited access, each user receives a small number of invitations they can share. Those invitations become socially valuable, particularly when demand is high enough that people begin reselling them.
What interests me is that Instinct is building distribution in a market where its competitors already have enormous distribution advantages.
Meta can place an agent in applications used by billions of people. Google has Android, Search, and Gmail. OpenAI has ChatGPT. Each has an existing relationship with users and access to infrastructure that a young startup has to build or acquire.
Instinct doesn't have those advantages. Its early growth depends on people finding the product valuable enough to introduce it to someone else.
That gives Shinn an unusual race to run: he needs to build a sufficiently strong user relationship before incumbent platforms make similar capabilities ubiquitous.
The question isn't only whether Instinct can acquire users. It's whether those users develop enough trust and dependency that an agent bundled into an existing platform becomes less attractive.
The interface isn't disappearing. It's changing sides.
There's a popular argument that AI agents will make interfaces obsolete. I'm sympathetic to it, but I think it's incomplete.
Interfaces exist partly because humans need ways to understand and manipulate complex systems. If an agent can perform those manipulations for us, we may no longer need to interact with the same interfaces directly. But the underlying complexity doesn't disappear. An agent still needs to understand permissions, handle errors, preserve state, recover from failed actions, and coordinate information across services.
In some respects, this makes software more complicated, not less.
Consider a travel booking. A person using a website can visually inspect available flights, compare prices, review the itinerary, and decide whether to purchase a ticket. An agent performing the same task needs to represent these decisions internally. It must know which preferences matter, when to request approval, and how to distinguish a successful booking from an incomplete transaction.
We've moved complexity away from the user, but someone still has to manage it. Microsoft's research on Hybrid Computer Use explores how agents can interact with software through programmatic tools, accessibility interfaces, and visual computer use, rather than relying on a single interaction method. [2]
This makes me wonder whether the next generation of software will have two distinct interfaces: one designed for people, and another designed for agents acting on their behalf.
And if agents become the primary consumers of software interfaces, the incentives for building applications may change considerably. A beautiful interface might become less important than reliable APIs, structured data, and predictable execution.
There's a certain irony in spending decades perfecting graphical user interfaces only to build software that operates them without us.
Trust might be the real moat
Instinct's growth is impressive, but the numbers I find more interesting concern trust.
In his interview, Shinn described how roughly 40% of users had shared a personal credit card with Instinct within three weeks, and how users who connected at least one piece of sensitive information showed around 80% retention. These are company-reported figures, but they're interesting signals about the relationship people are developing with their agents. [1]
A personal agent becomes more useful as it learns about your life. It might know which airlines you prefer, how you write emails, which brands you've worked with, and which tasks you tend to procrastinate on. More importantly, it can turn that knowledge into actions.
This creates a feedback loop. The more context the agent has, the less I need to explain. The less I need to explain, the more frequently I use it. Over time, switching to a different agent could mean losing the accumulated context that makes the experience useful.
But that same accumulation makes the potential consequences of failure more serious. A chatbot hallucinating a restaurant recommendation is annoying. An agent making a reservation on the wrong date is inconvenient. An agent with financial access making an unauthorized purchase is something else entirely.
I don't think these concerns are peripheral to the product. They're central to whether personal agents can become a mainstream category.
And perhaps this is where Instinct's distribution strategy becomes particularly interesting. Acquiring a user is one thing. Becoming the agent that person trusts with their finances, communications, preferences, and daily responsibilities is something else.
A larger company might be able to distribute a competing agent to billions of people overnight, but distribution does not automatically produce trust. That relationship has to be earned through repeated, successful interactions.
Of course, the opposite is also true. Trust can disappear remarkably quickly when a system makes a consequential mistake.
Maybe the most important feature is having fewer features
One thing I find refreshing about Instinct is that it doesn't ask me to learn an entirely new system.
Shinn has talked about building a personal assistant that can be reached through familiar forms of communication, including messages and phone calls, rather than requiring users to operate another application. [1]
I think there's a broader lesson here about product design. For years, software companies have competed by adding capabilities, and capabilities generally become features. More buttons, more settings, more dashboards, more things to customize.
But a product can become more capable without becoming more complicated to use. In fact, perhaps the most sophisticated thing about a good agent is how little of that sophistication the user needs to see.
Of course, there are limits. Sometimes I want to inspect the work, change a parameter, or understand why the agent made a particular decision. A conversation isn't always the best interface for complex information. So I don't think everything should become a chat box.
I think the more interesting possibility is that interfaces become something we request when they're useful, rather than something we're required to navigate before any work can happen.
The default interaction could be intent. The interface appears when the task calls for it.
The thing I'm actually excited about
I don't know whether Instinct will become the dominant personal agent, or whether this category will eventually be absorbed into the products we already use. There are enormous questions around reliability, cost, privacy, and how much autonomy people genuinely want to give their software.
I'm also conscious that being an early user of a new AI product is a fairly privileged perspective. Most people have neither the time nor the inclination to experiment with agents until they figure out how to make them useful. For personal agents to matter at scale, they need to work for people who don't spend their weekends reading about AI.
But I keep returning to the same observation.
For much of computing history, we've organized our work around the limitations of software. We learned which application to use, which sequence of actions to follow, and how to move information between systems that weren't designed to cooperate. We became operators of increasingly powerful tools.
Now we're beginning to build software that can operate those tools for us.
I still spend plenty of time correcting my agent, checking its work, and occasionally wondering what on earth it's doing. It is far from magic. But every so often, I ask it to do something that would previously have consumed an entire afternoon, and it just does it.
Then I find myself wondering why I ever thought the old way was normal.
I think Shinn is onto something with his thesis about personal agents becoming a new distribution layer for the internet. Whether Instinct ultimately wins that race is another question, especially with some of the largest technology companies in the world pursuing the same opportunity. But I find the possibility that a relatively small team could change how we interact with software genuinely exciting.
And on a slightly less philosophical note, I'm still very curious who Noah knows that helped him raise a billion dollars. I'd love to know.
References
[1] Shinn, N. (2026). Building Instinct: The Personal Agent. Invest Like the Best, Episode 493.
[2] Microsoft Research (2026). Hybrid Computer Use.
[3] Reuters (2026). AI Agent Firm Instinct Raises $1 Billion in Latest Funding Round.

writing.title: Was Lady Gaga's Meat Dress a Warning About AI?
writing.text:
I recently came across a blog post by Niklas Gruhn titled Don't Be a Meat Proxy, and I haven't stopped thinking about it.
The premise is wonderfully absurd. Someone asks a question in Slack, leaves feedback on a pull request, or starts an argument in a group chat. Instead of responding themselves, the other person copies the question into Claude, takes whatever comes back, and pastes it into the conversation. The recipient is now reading a response from an AI through a human who may not have understood, verified, or even read it.
Congratulations, you've become a meat proxy. A biological API endpoint with considerably worse latency.
It's a funny term, but I think it captures something much more interesting about how we're beginning to use AI. We've built systems that can generate increasingly sophisticated work with very little human involvement, but we haven't quite figured out what meaningful human involvement should look like anymore. Instead, we're creating workflows where the human is technically responsible for the output while contributing almost nothing to its production.
And somehow, we've started calling this productivity.
The illusion of getting more done
One of the stranger consequences of generative AI is how dramatically it has changed the relationship between effort and output. A report that might have taken hours to write can now be generated in minutes. A developer can produce hundreds of lines of code without understanding every implementation detail. Someone can respond to dozens of emails without writing a single sentence themselves.
There's nothing inherently wrong with this. In fact, eliminating unnecessary effort is one of the best things technology can do. I've spent plenty of time building automations to avoid repetitive work, and I use AI extensively in my own projects. But I think we're beginning to confuse the volume of work produced with the amount of useful work accomplished.
Consider a developer who receives a ticket, gives it to Claude Code, and submits the resulting pull request. Another developer reviews the implementation and points out a potential issue. The first developer copies the feedback into Claude, generates a fix, and pushes another commit. This repeats until the reviewer is satisfied.
From the outside, the original developer appears to have completed the task. They submitted the pull request, responded to feedback, and merged the implementation. Yet it's worth asking where the actual understanding occurred. The reviewer identified the problems, evaluated the implementation, and determined what needed to change. The coding agent produced the modifications. The developer connecting them may have contributed little beyond transferring information between the two.
This is close to the example Gruhn raises in his original essay, and I think it's especially interesting because the workflow technically functions. The code might even be good. The problem is that the person credited with the work may not be the person who understood it.
Of course, using AI to implement something doesn't automatically make someone a meat proxy. An experienced engineer might delegate most of the code generation while still making architectural decisions, evaluating trade-offs, and taking responsibility for the result. The distinction isn't how much code someone writes themselves. It's whether they understand and contribute to the work being produced.
We're accustomed to measuring productivity through visible artifacts: documents completed, messages answered, pull requests merged. Generative AI makes those artifacts extraordinarily cheap to produce, which means they become increasingly poor proxies for the value of the underlying work.
We've made writing cheaper than reading
For most of the internet's history, producing a substantial piece of writing required enough effort that its existence suggested at least some investment from the author. A detailed email, technical explanation, or lengthy proposal usually meant someone had spent time thinking through what they wanted to communicate.
That assumption is becoming less reliable.
An AI-generated response can be longer, more polished, and more technically elaborate than something a person would have written themselves. It can also contain far more information than the recipient needs. The sender saves time by generating it, but the recipient still has to read, interpret, and verify it.
We've reduced the cost of producing information without necessarily reducing the cost of consuming it.
Suppose I ask a colleague why a particular technical decision was made. They could spend five minutes explaining the reasoning in their own words, or they could ask Claude to generate a comprehensive explanation and send me several paragraphs. The second option might take them thirty seconds. But if I now have to spend ten minutes reading the response, separating relevant information from unnecessary detail, and checking whether it actually answers my question, the total amount of work hasn't decreased. It's simply been transferred to me.
It's a rather unfortunate trade. You save thirty minutes writing an essay nobody asked for, and I inherit the responsibility of figuring out what it means.
This is what I find most frustrating about unfiltered AI output. It often creates the appearance of thoroughness while making the actual exchange of information less efficient. A useful response is not necessarily the most comprehensive response. Sometimes the most valuable thing someone can do is understand a complicated issue well enough to explain it simply.
That requires judgment. And judgment is precisely what disappears when a person forwards model output without processing it.
The human in the loop might just be the bottleneck
There's another irony here. We're building increasingly autonomous agents, but many workflows still require humans to manually transfer information between systems.
An agent writes a document. A person copies it into another application. A second agent evaluates the document. The person returns the feedback to the first agent. The cycle continues until someone is satisfied.
Why is the human there?
Sometimes there's a good answer. The person may need to make a decision, authorize an action, or assess something the systems cannot reliably evaluate. Human oversight can be genuinely valuable when it involves meaningful judgment. But in other cases, the human is only present because the systems haven't been connected.
In software engineering, we generally wouldn't consider it good architecture to require a person to manually copy JSON responses between two services. We'd build an integration, define an interface, and let the systems communicate. Yet we routinely create equivalent workflows with AI agents and call them human-in-the-loop systems.
We've somehow reinvented middleware, except the middleware needs coffee breaks and occasionally forgets to reply.
This reminds me of a much older observation by Lisanne Bainbridge in her 1983 paper Ironies of Automation. Bainbridge argued that automating routine parts of a system can leave humans responsible for the very situations they are least prepared to handle. As automation improves, the remaining human role often becomes more difficult rather than less important. [2]
I think we're encountering a related problem with AI agents. We keep humans involved because we want the reassurance of human oversight, but the mere presence of a human doesn't guarantee that any meaningful oversight is happening.
Research on human involvement in automated decision-making adds another interesting complication. In Putting a Human in the Loop: Increasing Uptake, but Decreasing Accuracy of Automated Decision-Making, Sele and Chugunova found that allowing people to adjust algorithmic recommendations increased their willingness to use the system, but their interventions also reduced average prediction accuracy in the experiment. The researchers observed that participants tended to follow algorithmic recommendations more closely than equivalent human recommendations. [3]
I find this particularly interesting because it challenges the assumption that adding a human necessarily makes an automated system more reliable. We often treat human oversight as a safeguard, but its effectiveness depends on whether the person can independently assess the system's recommendation.
A reviewer who doesn't understand the implementation they're approving isn't much of a safeguard. Neither is an employee who automatically accepts an agent's recommendation because it looks plausible.
The useful human role should be explicit. What decision is this person making? What information do they have that the agent doesn't? What would cause them to reject the proposed action?
If we can't answer those questions, there's a reasonable chance we've inserted a person into the workflow without giving them a meaningful function.
The problem isn't delegation. It's responsibility.
I don't think the solution is to use AI less. That would be a strange conclusion to draw from technology that can already perform so many useful tasks.
The distinction I care about is between delegating execution and delegating judgment.
When I use an agent to research companies, organize information, or draft outreach, I'm delegating work that would otherwise require considerable manual effort. But I still need to decide which companies matter, whether the research is credible, and what I actually want to communicate.
Those decisions are often the most valuable part of the process.
There's an important difference between asking AI to help formulate an argument and asking AI to decide what your argument should be. The former can make your thinking more effective. The latter can make it surprisingly easy to stop thinking altogether.
This is especially apparent in writing. Language models are remarkably good at producing explanations that sound reasonable, even when the underlying reasoning is weak or the author hasn't fully understood the subject. A well-written paragraph creates an impression of competence. We've spent our entire lives using language as a signal of understanding, and now we've built systems capable of producing that signal without requiring understanding from the person presenting it.
The danger isn't necessarily that the AI is wrong. It might be completely correct. The problem is that the human presenting the information may have no independent basis for evaluating it.
This creates a peculiar accountability problem. When someone sends me a technical recommendation, I normally assume they're prepared to explain why they believe it. I can question their assumptions, ask about alternatives, and understand the reasoning behind their conclusion.
But if the recommendation is generated by a model they haven't evaluated, that conversation becomes difficult. They may simply return to the model, ask it to defend its earlier answer, and forward the response. At that point, I'm not really having a discussion with another person. I'm having a discussion with a language model through someone who controls the prompt but doesn't necessarily understand the subject.
Which raises the rather obvious question of why I wasn't invited to speak to Claude directly.
Doing less should mean understanding more
I think one of the most important skills in an AI-heavy workplace will be knowing which parts of a task deserve your attention.
It's unrealistic to expect people to personally verify every line of code, every data transformation, or every intermediate step of a sufficiently complex agentic workflow. The entire point of automation is to reduce how much work requires direct human attention. But we need better ways to determine where that attention is most valuable.
For a software engineer, that might mean spending less time implementing boilerplate and more time understanding architecture, testing assumptions, and evaluating whether the system behaves correctly. For someone working in product, it might mean delegating research synthesis while retaining responsibility for deciding which customer problems are worth solving.
The objective isn't to preserve human effort for its own sake. It's to make sure we're applying human effort where it changes the outcome.
This is also why I think the ability to explain your work will become increasingly important. If you've delegated an implementation to an agent but can explain its architecture, identify its limitations, and defend the decisions it embodies, you've probably contributed something meaningful. If your only response to a question is to ask the agent what it thinks, the situation is different.
Of course, explanation isn't a perfect measure of understanding. People can produce convincing explanations for things they don't understand, and AI can help them do that too. But being able to reason independently about the work is still a useful standard.
There's also a broader question about how we develop expertise. If we increasingly delegate implementation, drafting, and analysis, we may reduce our exposure to the practical details through which expertise is acquired. The relationship isn't straightforward. AI can also be a remarkably effective teacher, and someone who actively interrogates an agent's work might learn faster than someone doing everything manually.
What matters is whether the interaction involves learning and evaluation or simply accepting whatever appears on the screen.
A person who uses AI to understand an unfamiliar concept is doing something different from a person who uses AI to avoid understanding it.
Maybe we haven't redefined work yet
I think meat proxy resonates because it gives a name to something we've all started encountering, but haven't quite figured out how to talk about.
We're in an awkward transitional period where the tools can perform substantial portions of knowledge work, while our expectations of what it means to contribute haven't changed nearly as quickly.
We still reward people for producing artifacts, even when producing those artifacts no longer requires much effort. We still assign ownership based on who submitted the work, rather than who exercised judgment over it. And we still treat human involvement as inherently valuable, even when that involvement consists entirely of forwarding information between systems.
This doesn't mean AI-generated work is less valuable. In many cases, it's an extraordinary improvement. But it does mean we need to become more precise about what people are contributing.
A developer who uses AI to ship a reliable system is not necessarily less valuable than one who writes every line themselves. A researcher who uses AI to investigate more hypotheses may be doing better research. Someone who automates an entire administrative workflow may create far more value than someone who performs those tasks manually.
The common factor isn't the amount of effort they personally expend. It's whether they exercise judgment, take responsibility for the outcome, and contribute something the system would not otherwise have produced.
I also think there's a social dimension that gets overlooked. When someone asks a colleague a question, they may not just be requesting information. They may want that person's experience, opinion, or perspective. Replacing the response with a generic AI explanation can miss the entire point of the interaction.
If I wanted to know what Claude thinks, I could ask Claude. When I ask another person, I'm usually interested in what they think.
Don't outsource the part that makes you useful
I don't particularly care whether someone uses AI to write code, draft emails, or produce documents. I do all of those things myself, and I think we're only beginning to understand how much work these systems can take off our hands.
What I care about is whether the person using the tool is still participating intellectually in the process.
There's a difference between being the person who decides what should happen and being the person who forwards what a model decided should happen. As AI becomes capable of handling more execution, I suspect that distinction will become increasingly important.
The opportunity is enormous. We can spend less time on repetitive implementation and more time making decisions, exploring ideas, and solving problems that previously required too much manual work. But that only happens if we use the time we've recovered to do something more valuable.
Otherwise, we end up in a strange situation where everyone is producing more work, everyone is reading more work, and nobody is particularly sure who's doing the thinking.
Perhaps the most useful question to ask before sending something AI-generated isn't whether the output is good enough to pass along. It's whether you've added anything by being the person who sends it.
Because if all you're doing is passing information between a person and a language model, congratulations. We've finally found a way to make computers faster by putting a human in the middle.
